migrationNotes: SPINE: A shop window is smashed and the staff tell the story three ways. Follow one sentence through three edits, putting the actor first, unburying the action from a noun and cutting the padding, and count the words each edit saves.

lesson.title: Actors and actions

steps.headline: Who did it, and where the sentence says so

lead.text: Almost every sentence about an event has an actor, the person or thing that did it, and a receiver, the person or thing it was done to. In “The dog ate the sandwich”, the dog is the actor and the sandwich is the receiver. English lets you tell the story from either end. “The sandwich was eaten by the dog” describes the same event with the receiver in front.

The first version is in the active voice, which means the subject does the action. The second is in the passive voice, where the subject receives it. The passive is built from a form of “be” and a past participle, here “was eaten”, and the actor moves into a phrase that begins with “by” or drops out of the sentence.

afterFigure.text: Notice what else changed. The passive sentence is two words longer, and it opens with the sandwich, which the reader meets before knowing why it matters. The active sentence puts the doer first and gets on with the story.

lead.text: Back to the smashed window. Tell the first answer the other way round.

The passive does something else that is easy to miss. The actor sits in an optional “by” phrase, so it can be left out without a trace. “The sandwich was eaten” is a complete sentence, and it does not say by whom. That helps when nobody knows who acted, or when the actor does not matter. It also lets a writer avoid naming someone, which is why you meet sentences such as “The decision was taken to close the office.”

So ask of any passive sentence who did this, and whether the reader should know. If the actor matters, bring it forward into the subject. The active version usually saves words as well, because the passive needs a form of “be” and often a “by”, and those add two words that the actor's name does not need.

afterFigure.text: The passive is not wrong. It earns its place when the receiver is the point of the sentence. The skill is knowing which sentences are hiding someone.

steps.headline: Make “The report was written by the analyst” active.

lead.text: Three moves turn a passive into an active sentence.

workedSteps.text: Find the actor. The “by” phrase names the analyst.
Make the actor the subject: “The analyst”.
Turn “was written” into a plain past verb and keep the receiver as its object: “The analyst wrote the report.”

steps.headline: Make “Mistakes were made by the finance office” active.

lead.text: The passive can delete the actor altogether. That is honest when nobody knows who acted, and evasive when the writer does.

reveal.text: The actor was in the sentence all along, hidden behind “by”. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?

workedSteps.text: The receiver is “mistakes”, and the verb is “were made”.
The actor is named inside the “by” phrase.
Move the actor to the front. Which words become the subject?

lead.text: Rewrite the sentence, then count what your version needs.

reveal.text: You moved the actor to the front and dropped “was” and “by”. The passive's extra words disappeared, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.

steps.headline: A noun that hides a verb

lead.text: The passive is one way for a sentence to lose its energy. A second way is to take an action and turn it into a noun. “Approve” is a verb: “The board approved the plan.” Turn it into the noun “approval” and the sentence needs another verb to carry it: “The board gave approval to the plan.” The action is still there, but it sits inside a noun while “gave” does almost nothing.
A noun made from a verb in this way is a nominalisation. Common endings are -tion, -ment, -al and -ance, as in “announcement”, “arrival”, “performance” and “agreement”.

afterFigure.text: The repair is to turn the noun back into a verb. “The board gave approval to the plan” has seven words and “The board approved the plan” has five. Look for a weak verb such as “gave”, “made”, “took” or “conducted” holding up a noun that is really an action. Remove both and the action takes over the sentence.

lead.text: This sentence buries two verbs. Count the words before and after.

reveal.text: You turned two noun phrases back into verbs. Fewer words, and the committee now does something.

lead.text: A sentence can lose force in a third way, through padding. Some words add nothing a reader would miss. A frame such as “it is a fact that” only announces that a claim is coming, and the claim could simply arrive. Some modifiers repeat what the noun already says, as in “a free gift”, since a gift is free already. Phrases such as “at this point in time” take five words to say “now”.

Cutting these is the easiest edit to count. Read the sentence, mark the words you could remove without changing what it claims, and subtract. If the claim survives the cut, the words were padding. If something went missing, put it back.

afterFigure.text: Padding often goes with the other two faults. A writer who is unsure of the claim reaches for a frame, and a writer who avoids naming the actor reaches for a long phrase. Cutting padding is often the first step towards seeing who is acting.

lead.text: Here is one sentence through the edits. “The delivery of the parcels was completed by the courier on Monday” has twelve words. Put the courier first and you get “The courier completed the delivery of the parcels on Monday”, which has ten. Unbury the verb inside “delivery” and you get “The courier delivered the parcels on Monday”, which has seven.

Five words went, and nothing the reader needed went with them. Each edit gave something back as well. The first restored a name, and the second restored a verb that moves. Put the actor first and the action in the verb, then cut whatever carries nothing.

afterFigure.text: The order of the edits does not matter much. What matters is that you ask of a sentence who acts and where the action is, and then which words could go.

segments.text: The courier delivered the parcels on Monday,

lead.text: The frame and three of the modifiers in this sentence can go. Count the sentence before you cut.

reveal.text: The claim stayed and ten words went. A revision that loses words and keeps the claim is an improvement you can measure.

lesson.orientation: Move actors into subjects and actions into verbs. Switch between active and passive, unbury nominalisations and count the words a revision saves.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: A shop owner arrives to find the front window smashed and asks the staff what happened. One of them says, “The window was broken by Sam.” Another says, “The window got broken.” Both describe the same event in nearly the same words, yet the owner learns something different from each. The first answer names a person. The second leaves a gap where the person should be.

Where a name sits in a sentence, and whether it appears at all, is something a writer controls. Put the person who acts first and the sentence moves. Bury the action inside a noun and it sags. Business reports, official letters and school essays are full of sentences that do the second, and most can be repaired in seconds once you know what to look for.
We start with the smashed window and then work through longer sentences, counting the words each repair saves.

diagram.alt: Two ways of reporting a smashed shop window. In one, Sam is drawn as the person who broke it. In the other, an empty dashed circle stands where the person should be.
diagram.caption: Both answers describe the same broken window. Only the first says who is responsible.

intro.promise: By the end you'll move actors into subjects and unbury actions from nouns, counting the words each revision saves.

recap.keyIdea: Make the actor the subject and the action the verb. Unbury verbs from nouns and cut words that carry no meaning.

blocks.text: You put the actor first in a sentence about a smashed window, then did the same for a motion, a report and a finance office. You unburied two verbs and saved five words, and you cut a sixteen-word sentence down to six.

recap.nextHook: Clear sentences carry arguments, and the next lesson starts with a friend who says you should get a dog because hers makes her so happy.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'The motion was rejected by the committee' in the active voice. How many words does the active sentence have?
hints: Make the actor, the committee, the subject.
Use the past-tense verb without 'was', and drop 'by'.
Count every word, including both articles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive took seven.

questions.onCorrect: Five words: “The committee rejected the motion.” The actor leads and the passive's extra words go.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Rewrite it with the committee acting, then count.
Drop both “was” and “by”: the participle becomes a plain past verb.
You have lost a word. Count both articles.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'Mistakes were made by the finance office' in the active voice. What becomes the subject?
hints: Find the 'by' phrase: whoever sits inside it performed the action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The finance office made mistakes.' The actor, hidden in the 'by' phrase, moves into the subject position.

questions.onCorrect: The finance office made mistakes. The actor, hidden in the “by” phrase, moves into the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: “Mistakes” is the receiver. In the active sentence it follows the verb.

questions.prompt: Unbury the verbs in 'The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy': 'made a decision' becomes 'decided' and 'conduct a review of' becomes 'review'. How many words does the revision save?
hints: Count the words in the original sentence.
Write out the revision and count it.
Subtract the revised count from the original count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve words become seven: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' Five are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve words become seven, so the revision saves five. Buried verbs cost words and force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. The question asks how many words the revision saves.
That is the length of the revision. Subtract it from the original.
Recount each sentence one word at a time, then check the subtraction.

questions.prompt: Cut the empty frame 'In my opinion, it is true that' and the redundant words 'personal', 'basically' and 'final' from 'In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.' How many words remain?
hints: Count the original sentence first.
Count the frame words and the redundant words you are removing.
Subtract, then check by reading what is left aloud.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sixteen words lose ten: 'The outcome depends on the weather.' Six remain.

questions.onCorrect: Six words remain: sixteen lose ten. Cutting padding keeps the claim and loses only noise.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the words you cut. Count what is left.
That is the original length. Remove the frame and the repeated words first.
Check that you removed every word listed, including the three modifiers.

questions.prompt: 'The budget was approved by the council in March.' How many words does the active version save?
hints: Put the council in the subject position.
Write the active sentence and count it.
Subtract the active count from the passive count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine words become seven: 'The council approved the budget in March.' Two are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Nine words become seven, so two are saved. Moving the actor forward drops “was” and “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Count the active version and subtract.
That is the active sentence's length. The question asks how many words are saved.

questions.prompt: 'An investigation of the causes was carried out by the board.' Which verb is buried inside the noun 'investigation'?
hints: Remove the noun ending '-ation' and rebuild the verb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Investigate': 'The board investigated the causes' turns the noun back into a verb and the board into the subject.

questions.onCorrect: “Investigation” hides the verb “investigate”. Turn it back and the board becomes the actor.

misconceptions.feedback: “Carried out” is the weak verb propping the noun up. Look inside the noun itself.

questions.prompt: “The window was broken by Sam.” Say it so that Sam comes first. How many words does your sentence have?
hints: Start with Sam. What did Sam do?
Turn “was broken” into one plain past verb.
Count every word, including “the”.
questions.onCorrect: Four words: “Sam broke the window.” Putting the actor first drops “was” and “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the original. Rewrite it with Sam acting, then count.
Drop both “was” and “by”: “broken” becomes a plain past verb.
You have lost a word. Check that “the” is still there.

questions.prompt: In “The pitch was flooded by the storm”, which word names the actor?
hints: Look inside the “by” phrase.
questions.onCorrect: The storm did the flooding. In the passive the actor moves into a “by” phrase, and the receiver becomes the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The pitch receives the action. Find the one that does it.
“Flooded” is the action itself. Ask who or what did it.

questions.prompt: Why does the active version read as stronger?

acceptedIdeas: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The actor leads and the verb is shorter.

choices.label: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
It is longer, so it carries more detail.

questions.onCorrect: The actor leads and the verb is direct, so the sentence says who did what in fewer words.

misconceptions.feedback: It is shorter, not longer. The extra words in the passive carry nothing.
Not always. The passive suits cases where the actor is unknown or does not matter.

questions.prompt: Which sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb: “A review of the rules was undertaken by the staff”?
hints: Two things have to change: who leads, and where the action sits.

choices.label: The staff undertook a review of the rules.
The rules were reviewed by the staff.

questions.onCorrect: “Reviewed” turns the buried noun back into a verb, and the staff acts as subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The staff are now the subject, but the action is still buried in a noun.
The verb is restored, but the sentence is still passive, so the receiver leads.

questions.prompt: Which noun buries the verb in “The board gave a refusal of the request”?
hints: Look for an action word that has become a noun.
questions.onCorrect: “A refusal” is the action turned into a noun, and “gave” is a weak verb carrying it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Request” names what was refused. Find the noun that is really an action.
“Board” is the actor. The buried verb is hidden in an action noun.
